parts.title: `const`, and how TypeScript decides a variable's type

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 2 - TypeScript - `const`, and how TypeScript decides a variable's type

Every locator from here on gets assigned to a `const`. This is a full primer on why, and
on the type-inference rule that means you never write `: Locator` by hand.

> **Every run starts fresh.** Each time you press Run, your code starts from a clean slate. Nothing from a previous run is still in memory.

| # | Concept | Why today needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `const` | every `page.locator()` call gets assigned to one |
| 2 | Dynamic vs static typing, and inference | why `const box = page.locator(...)` needs no type annotation |

## 1. `const`

`const` declares a variable that **cannot be reassigned** — you can't point it at a
different value later. It says nothing about whether the *thing itself* can change.

**Expected:** `[ 1, 2, 3, 4 ]`.

`push()` mutated the array in place — `numbers` was never reassigned, so `const` never
objected. This is exactly the shape of a locator: the `const` itself never changes, but
the element it points at (checked, filled, removed from the DOM) does.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same rule, a different container: declare a `const` object with two properties, change one of them, and print it — the object mutates and `const` says nothing. Then add a line that points the same `const` at a brand-new object and read the error TypeScript gives you.

blocks.text:
## Where this shows up: `page.locator()`

```ts
const emailBox = page.locator("input[type='email']");
```

`emailBox` is a **reference** to "whatever matches this selector right now" — not a
snapshot of one element. `const` fits because you never point `emailBox` at a different
locator; you just call methods on it (`.fill()`, `.check()`) that act on the live page.
The TypeScript-only stand-in below shows the same idea without a browser.
**Expected:** `{ selector: "input[type='email']", timesClicked: 2 }`.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same stand-in, one more method: add a `pretendFill(loc, value)` that stores the value on the object, call it once, and print the object. Two methods have now changed its contents and the `const` still has never been reassigned.

blocks.text:
## 2. Dynamic vs static typing — why no `: Locator` was written

TypeScript is **statically typed**: every variable's type is fixed at compile time, and
`tsc` checks it before your code ever runs. You almost never *write* the type, though —
TypeScript **infers** it from whatever you assign.

| | Static typing (TypeScript) | Dynamic typing (plain JavaScript) |
|---|---|---|
| When the type is decided | at compile time, and fixed | at run time, and can change |
| Who catches a type mistake | `tsc`, before you run anything | nobody — you find out when it crashes |
| `const x = "hi"; x = 5;` | compile error | runs; `x` is now a number |

One line for context: this differs from a language like Java, where you write the type
yourself every time — `String x = "hi";`.

**Expected:** `string number number`.

`name` and `count` got their types from the value to the right of `=` — that's inference.
`anything: any` is how you'd *turn off* static typing for one variable; later days show
why that's usually a bad idea. `page.locator(...)` is inferred as `Locator` the exact
same way `"Ada"` was inferred as `string` — TypeScript looks up what `.locator()` returns
and assigns that type to your `const`, with zero annotation from you.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

variation.prompt: Same inference, different types: declare a `const` boolean and a `const` array of strings, neither annotated, and print `typeof` each — note that the array reports `object`, because `typeof` predates arrays having their own answer. Then try pushing a number into the string array and read which line `tsc` refuses.

blocks.text:
## Recap

| Concept | Remember |
|---|---|
| `const` | can't reassign the variable; the value it points at can still mutate |
| Static typing | `tsc` fixes and checks every type before your code runs |
| Inference | TypeScript reads the type off the assigned value — you rarely annotate |

**Next:** [Day 2.2 — XPath, CSS, and your first real assertions](/learn/w2/d2/p2)
`const numbers = [1, 2, 3];` followed by `numbers.push(4);` — does that compile?

options: No — `const` makes the array read-only, so `push` is refused
Yes — `const` stops you pointing `numbers` at a different array; it does not freeze the array's contents
Yes, but only because the array was annotated `number[]`
checkpoint.explanation: `const` is about the binding, not the value. `push` mutates the array in place and `numbers` still points at the same array, so nothing is reassigned. This is exactly the shape of a locator: the `const` is fixed, the element it refers to is not.

blocks.text: Why does `const emailBox = page.locator("input[type='email']")` need no `: Locator` annotation?

options: Because TypeScript infers the type from what `.locator()` returns
Because locators are exempt from type checking
Because `const` declarations are never type-checked, only `let` ones are
checkpoint.explanation: Inference: TypeScript reads the type off the right-hand side, exactly as it decided `const name = "Ada"` was a `string`. The type is still static and still checked — you just did not have to type it out.

parts.title: XPath, CSS, and your first real assertions

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 2 - Fundamentals - XPath, CSS, and your first real assertions

By the end of this lesson you will have located an element with both XPath and CSS,
assigned it to a `const` locator, and written your first real `expect()` assertions
against a real page.

| | |
|---|---|
| **You'll use** | `xpath=//tag[@attr='v']` · `tag[attr='v']` · `expect().toContainText()` · `.toHaveValue()` · `.toHaveURL()` |
| **Assumes** | [const and type inference](/learn/w2/d2/p1) · [locators](/learn/w1/d4/p2) |
| **Mode** | mixed — locator syntax runs live, but `expect()` only retries inside the test runner, so assertions go into a spec |
| **The shift** | [Day 1](/learn/w2/d1/p2) could only prove nothing threw. From here a test can fail for the right reason. |

> **Partly here, partly in your own project.** Locator syntax is explored live. Real `expect()` assertions —
> `toContainText`, `toHaveValue`, `toHaveURL` — only retry inside the test runner, so
> those get written to a spec, same as every day so far.

## XPath: absolute vs relative

| | Absolute | Relative |
|---|---|---|
| Starts with | `/html/body/div[1]/...` | `//tag[@attribute='value']` |
| Fragile? | yes — one inserted `<div>` breaks it | no — matches anywhere in the document |
| Use it | never | when nothing else identifies the element cleanly |

Always write relative XPath (`//...`). Absolute XPath is shown here only so you recognize
it and know to avoid it.

## CSS locator syntax, for contrast

| | XPath | CSS |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax | `//tag[@attribute='value']` | `tag[attribute='value']` |
| Prefix | `//` and `@` | neither |
| Can it go **up** the DOM (parent, ancestor) | yes | no |
| Can it go **sideways** (sibling) | yes | only "next sibling" (`+`) |

Playwright reaches for `getByRole`/`getByLabel`/`getByPlaceholder` before either of these
— [Week 1, Day 4.2](/learn/w1/d4/p2) covered why. XPath and CSS are for when
nothing on the element identifies it cleanly, which is common on older apps like today's.

**Expected:** both print `1` — same element, two syntaxes. The only differences: XPath
needs the `xpath=` prefix and an `@` before the attribute name; CSS needs neither.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

await page.goto("https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html");

Both should print 1 — and the pair of expressions should look exactly as different as the table said they would.

blocks.text:
## Assigning a locator to `const`

[Day 2.1](/learn/w2/d2/p1) is the full primer — the one-line version: the locator reference
is never reassigned, so it's always `const`.

**Expected:** `"Automation Demo Site "` — note the trailing space baked into the real
markup. [Day 3](/learn/w2/d3/p2) comes back to exactly this.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
blocks.starter:
const { browser, page } = await launch();
await page.goto("https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html");

variation.prompt: Same idea, a different element: assign the Refresh button (`#Button1`) to a `const` and print its `textContent()` wrapped in `JSON.stringify()`. Note the exact string, stray whitespace and all, before you ever write an assertion against it.

blocks.text:
## Your first real assertions

`expect()` **retries** against a locator until it matches or times out (5s default) —
unlike a plain `if`, which checks once. It only works inside the test runner, so from
here every assertion gets written into a spec.

| Matcher | Checks | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `toContainText(text)` | locator's text includes `text` | partial match |
| `toHaveValue(text)` | a form control's current value | exactly what you just filled |
| `toHaveURL(pattern)` | the page's current URL | confirming navigation happened — or didn't |

**Expected result:** `1 passed`.

Two things worth noticing:

- `toContainText("Automation Demo Site")` passes even though the real heading has a
  trailing space — Playwright's text matchers **normalize whitespace** before comparing.
  [Day 3](/learn/w2/d3/p2) shows where that normalization does *not* happen (raw XPath).
- `toHaveURL(/Register\.html/)` after clicking Submit is the honest assertion for this
  app. It was verified there is no confirmation page, no modal, and no navigation on
  submit — so the lesson asserts what's actually true instead of an invented "thank
  you" page.

## Best practices

- Prefer relative XPath and role/label locators over absolute XPath — never ship absolute XPath.
- Use `toHaveText` only when you know the *exact* string; default to `toContainText`.
- Assert something observable — a value, a URL, a text fragment — not just "didn't throw."

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute XPath (`/html/body/div[1]/...`) | passes today, breaks on the next markup tweak | write `//tag[@attr='value']` instead |
| Assuming Submit navigates | a `toHaveURL` assertion for a "thank you" page times out | verified: this app's Submit stays put — assert on filled values instead |
| Calling `expect()` in a lesson cell | throws — no test runner behind it | write it to a `.spec.ts`, as above |
Which XPath belongs in code you intend to keep?

options: `/html/body/div[1]/div[2]/form/input[3]` — it is the most precise
`//input[@type='email']` — it matches anywhere in the document
Either; they are two spellings of the same thing
checkpoint.explanation: An absolute path encodes the whole document structure, so one inserted `<div>` anywhere above your element breaks it. A relative XPath matches on the element's own attributes and survives the markup moving. The lesson shows absolute XPath only so you recognise it and avoid it.

blocks.text: What does `expect(locator).toContainText("Demo")` do that a plain `if (text.includes("Demo"))` does not?

options: It retries until the locator matches or it times out
It searches the whole page rather than one element
It is case-insensitive
checkpoint.explanation: Web assertions retry for 5 seconds by default, which is what makes them safe against a page that has not finished rendering. A plain `if` checks once, right now, and a page that needed another 200ms fails for no real reason. Retrying is also why `expect()` needs the test runner behind it.

blocks.text: The real heading on the page is `"Automation Demo Site "` — with a trailing space. Why does `toContainText("Automation Demo Site")` pass anyway?

options: Because `toContainText` only checks that the text starts with the string
Because Playwright's text matchers normalise whitespace before comparing
Because the assertion retried until the space was removed
checkpoint.explanation: Text matchers normalise whitespace, so the trailing space never reaches the comparison. Worth knowing precisely because it is not universal — [Day 3](/learn/w2/d3/p2) shows where that normalisation does *not* happen, and the raw string bites.

blocks.text:
- Relative XPath (`//tag[@attr='v']`) always; absolute XPath never.
- XPath can go up and sideways in the DOM; CSS can only go down and to the next sibling. That is the one real reason to reach for XPath.
- `expect()` **retries**; a plain `if` checks once. That is the whole difference, and it only works inside the test runner.
- `toContainText` for a fragment, `toHaveText` only when you know the exact string. Text matchers normalise whitespace.
- Assert something observable. "It didn't throw" is not an assertion.

## What's next

[Day 2.3](/learn/w2/d2/p3) wraps these assertions in a reusable function, the way Day 1.3 did for actions.

parts.title: The same assertions, wrapped for reuse

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 2 - Implementation - The same assertions, wrapped for reuse

By the end of this lesson you will have wrapped yesterday's `expect()` calls in one
function two different tests both call, extending [Day 1.3](/learn/w2/d1/p3)'s helper file.

> **No new API here on purpose.** Everything below is something you already ran in
> [Day 2.2](/learn/w2/d2/p2).

| | |
|---|---|
| **New API** | none — every line ran in [Day 2.2](/learn/w2/d2/p2) |
| **What changes** | three repeated `expect()` calls become one `expectFormFilledCorrectly(page, email)` |
| **Builds on** | [Day 1.3](/learn/w2/d1/p3)'s helper file, which now holds an action helper *and* a check helper |

## The problem with what we wrote yesterday

If three tests each need to confirm the form accepted its data, that's the same three
`expect()` calls copy-pasted three times — and a renamed field means fixing it in three places.

## Same code, with structure around it

| In Day 2.2 you wrote | Here it becomes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| three separate `expect(...)` calls inline in the test | one call: `await expectFormFilledCorrectly(page, email)` | the checks live in one place, reusable by every test that fills this form |

**This is still a function, not a page object.** A real page object (week 3) is a
`class` that **never** asserts — actions and checks stay separate. The helper below is a
different, equally common pattern: a **shared assertion helper**, and it's allowed to
assert because that is its entire job.

**Expected result:** `2 passed`. Both tests share the same three checks; a fourth test
that needs them gets them for free.

## What a reviewer would look for

- The repeated `expect()` calls live in one function, not copy-pasted across tests.
- It's clearly named as a checker (`expectFormFilledCorrectly`), not an action.
- It's kept separate from `fillRegistrationForm` — actions and checks are two different functions, not one that does both.
A page object must never assert. So why is `expectFormFilledCorrectly` allowed to be nothing but `expect()` calls?

options: Because it is a different pattern — a shared assertion helper, where asserting is the entire job
Because the no-assertions rule only applies once you are using classes in week 3
Because `toHaveValue` is exempt; only `toHaveURL` is banned from a page object
checkpoint.explanation: The rule is about keeping actions and checks in separate places, not about banning assertions from helpers. A page object holds the actions; a shared assertion helper holds the checks. What would be wrong is one function that fills the form *and* asserts on it.

blocks.text: Your suite has three tests that each fill this form and check it was accepted. The Email field is renamed. How many places should need editing?

options: Three — once per test
Two — the action helper and the assertion helper
Six — each test's fill and its assertion
checkpoint.explanation: That is the point of both of today's helpers: the locator appears once in `fillRegistrationForm` and once in `expectFormFilledCorrectly`, no matter how many tests call them. Inline, the same rename would be six edits and you would miss one.

blocks.text:
- Copy-pasted `expect()` calls are the same problem as copy-pasted actions, with the same fix: put them in one function.
- Name a checker for what it checks (`expectFormFilledCorrectly`), so a reader can tell at the call site that nothing is being *done* to the page.
- Keep actions and checks in separate functions. Week 3 formalises that split into a class; the discipline is identical today.

## What's next

[Day 2.4](/learn/w2/d2/p4) — your turn, with no worked examples to lean on.

# Week 2 - Day 2 - Practice - XPath, CSS, and assertions

Three problems, getting harder. No answer key.

Write spec files into `week2/generated/` and run them with `npx playwright test`.

> Struggling for more than about twenty minutes on one problem means the gap is in
> [Day 2.1](/learn/w2/d2/p1) or [Day 2.2](/learn/w2/d2/p2). Go back, re-read, come here again.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Three problems** | XPath by hand, then assertions, then a helper of your own |
| **Pulls on** | [Day 2.1](/learn/w2/d2/p1) for `const` · [Day 2.2](/learn/w2/d2/p2) for matchers · [Day 2.3](/learn/w2/d2/p3) for the shape |
| **Watch for** | an assertion that passes for the wrong reason — it is the failure mode this whole day exists to fix |

## When you are done

Look back at your Problem 3 helper and Day 1.3's action helper side by side: two
functions, two jobs, one file. That separation is most of what week 3 formalizes into a
class.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Locate the Refresh button with a relative XPath expression (not CSS,
not `getByRole`), assign it to a `const`, and assert its visible text with `toContainText`.

**Where.** A spec in `week2/generated/`.

**How you will know it worked.** `npx playwright test` reports `1 passed`.

> **Hint** — the button's own `id` from Day 1.2's probing was `Button1`.

**What to build.** Fill out the whole registration form (reuse [Day 1.3](/learn/w2/d1/p3)'s
helper or write your own), then assert on at least three different field values with
`toHaveValue`, plus one `toHaveURL` assertion confirming Submit didn't navigate away.

**Where.** A spec in `week2/generated/`.

**How you will know it worked.** All assertions pass on the first run — if one is flaky, you likely asserted on something this app doesn't actually guarantee.

**What to build.** Add a second assertion helper function to
`week2/generated/registration-helpers.ts` — for example one that checks a chosen skill
and country were actually selected — then a spec that imports and calls it.

**Where.** `week2/generated/registration-helpers.ts`, plus a spec in `week2/generated/`.

**How you will know it worked.** The new function contains only `expect()` calls, no
`.fill()`/`.check()`/`.selectOption()` — keep actions and checks in separate functions.
